categories.title: AR. Argument structure and decomposition rules

categories.index_title: SU. Sufficiency, uncertainty, and pitfall guidance
categories.title: SU. Sufficiency, uncertainty, and pitfall rules

categories.description: These guideline entries identify reasoning errors that weaken safety arguments. They are intended to support the development and review of safety cases by helping authors and reviewers examine whether claims, strategies, and evidence are argued soundly.
categories.title: LF. Logical fallacy rules

categories.description: These guideline entries identify presentation choices that affect how safety arguments are understood and reviewed. They help distinguish between wording that improves clarity and wording that increases confidence without increasing support.
categories.title: RD. Rhetorical device rules

guidelines.rationale: A safety case is built from claims that can be challenged, supported, or refuted. Statements that are merely labels, headings, slogans, or references are poor safety claims.
review_prompts: Could a reviewer tell what would make this claim false?
Is this a proposition, or only a topic label?
Is the claim understandable without extra interpretation?
guidelines.statement: State each claim as a sentence that can in principle be shown true or false.
guidelines.title: Write each claim as a falsifiable proposition

detection_hints: Look for goal text that is a noun phrase or topic label rather than a proposition.
Look for goals lacking a verb expressing a property or a measurable condition.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim text is a complete proposition that can be true or false.

guidelines.rationale: Bundled claims hide missing decomposition, make evidence assignment unclear, and produce review findings that are hard to localize.
review_prompts: Does the statement contain more than one property?
Would different evidence sets be needed for different parts of the claim?
Could one part of the statement be acceptable while another could fail?
guidelines.statement: Do not bundle multiple distinct properties, conclusions, or obligations into one goal.
guidelines.title: Put one main claim in one goal

detection_hints: Look for conjunctions linking distinct properties (safe and secure, complete and correct).
Look for goals where different properties would be supported by different evidence sets.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim asserts a single property or bundles several distinct properties.

guidelines.rationale: When a claim contains the whole story, reviewers cannot clearly see what is being claimed, what constrains the claim, and how the argument is intended to proceed. In GSN, that information should be visible in the structure, not hidden inside one sentence.
review_prompts: Is the goal text trying to describe both the claim and its decomposition?
Is scope that should be in context embedded in the claim text?
Are included topics listed in the claim instead of being expressed as sub-claims?
Would the argument become clearer if the parent claim were shortened and the included topics moved into strategy and child claims?
guidelines.statement: Do not pack argument structure, scope, decomposition topics, and caveats into a single claim. Keep the claim short, and express the rest through context, strategy, assumptions, and sub-claims.
guidelines.title: Avoid the essay-in-the-box

detection_hints: Look for claims that contain long comma-separated lists of topics.
Look for claim text that mixes scope, reasoning, caveats, and decomposition.
Look for phrases such as including, covering, considering, or with respect to introducing multiple subtopics.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim contains argument structure or scope that should be represented through context, strategy, assumptions, or sub-claims.
Check whether the claim lists child topics instead of making the decomposition visible in the argument structure.

guidelines.rationale: Ambiguous claims undermine review, traceability, and evidence relevance. This guideline directly supports UL 4600’s requirement to avoid substantive ambiguity in claims and arguments.
review_prompts: Could two competent reviewers understand the claim differently?
Is the object of the claim clear?
Is the property being claimed clear?
guidelines.statement: Write claims so that their meaning is clear enough that competent reviewers are likely to understand them in the same way.
guidelines.title: Avoid ambiguity and overloaded wording

detection_hints: Look for ambiguous subjects or properties (e.g. development is safe).
Look for claim text whose object or measured property is unclear.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether competent reviewers would interpret the claim consistently.

guidelines.rationale: Terms such as safe, timely, effective, normal, robust, all, every, and never can sound stronger or broader than the argument actually shows unless they are properly bounded.
review_prompts: Is the term bounded by context, lower-level argument, or linked criteria?
If safe is used, is it clear what safety judgment is being claimed at this level?
Is the scope of all, every, or never explicitly defined?
Would the claim remain reviewable if read on its own?
guidelines.statement: Do not leave broad evaluative terms or universal qualifiers unbounded. This includes terms such as safe, timely, effective, normal, robust, all, every, and never.
guidelines.title: Bound vague and universal qualifiers

detection_hints: Look for unbounded evaluative terms: safe, robust, effective, timely, normal.
Look for universal qualifiers without scope: all, every, never, always.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether evaluative or universal qualifiers in the claim are bounded by context or measurable criteria.

guidelines.rationale: These are different claim types with different evidence and different review questions.
review_prompts: Is this claim actually several claims chained together?
Would different teams or documents support different parts?
Should the branch be decomposed before evidence is attached?
guidelines.statement: Do not combine identification, adequacy, implementation, validation, and sufficiency in one claim unless the claim is intentionally kept at a higher level and the need for later decomposition is explicit
guidelines.title: Do not mix different logical steps in one claim

detection_hints: Look for claims that chain identification + implementation + validation in one sentence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim mixes identification, adequacy, implementation, validation, and sufficiency steps.

guidelines.rationale: When one assurance case element is used to do another element's job, the argument becomes harder to inspect, review, and challenge.
review_prompts: Is a claim carrying reasoning that belongs in an argument, strategy, or warrant?
Is local scope or meaning hidden inside the claim instead of being made explicit?
Is a dependency or rationale hidden in claim or argument text?
Is an evidence reference being used as if it were a claim?
Is a justification being used as if it were support?
guidelines.statement: Use the assurance case structure to make each element's role clear. Claims state propositions to be established; argument elements explain the reasoning, decomposition approach, or inference rule; context and assumptions define scope and dependencies when needed; and evidence elements identify the artefacts or observations used as support.
guidelines.title: Let structure carry the argument

detection_hints: Look for goals containing reasoning verbs (we argue that, by decomposing).
Look for solutions phrased as claims rather than evidence references.
Look for assumptions or justifications buried in claim or strategy text.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each element is used for its intended GSN role.

guidelines.rationale: A hidden reasoning step is a common source of argument gaps.
review_prompts: Is the decomposition rule visible?
Would another reviewer derive the same child-claim set?
Does the strategy explain why these children support this parent?
guidelines.statement: State how the parent claim is being decomposed or argued; do not make the reviewer infer the decomposition rule from wording alone.
guidelines.title: State the inference step explicitly

detection_hints: Look for branches with sub-claims but no strategy element explaining the decomposition rule.
Look for parent claims whose decomposition rule is implicit in the wording.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each decomposition has an explicit reasoning step stating how children support the parent.

guidelines.rationale: This keeps the claim interpretable and makes clear which information defines the claim's scope and meaning, and which conditions the argument depends on being true.
review_prompts: Is this text making the claim itself, defining the claim's scope, or stating a dependency that must hold?
Is any condition required for the claim to hold hidden in wording rather than made explicit?
Would the argument be clearer if scope, definitions, or dependencies were represented separately?
If context is included in claim text, is it deliberate, consistent, and necessary for the claim to be true or false?
guidelines.statement: Make scope, definitions, operating conditions, and dependencies explicit. Use separate context and assumption structures when supported by the notation or tool; where they must appear in claim text, write them deliberately and consistently rather than hiding them in ambiguous qualifiers.
guidelines.title: Use context and assumptions deliberately

detection_hints: Look for claim text containing scope phrases (in ODD X, during mode Y) or dependency phrases (with valid Z).

suggested_checks.description: Check whether scope and dependencies in claim text should be moved to context or assumption elements.

guidelines.rationale: Top-level claims need readability and stability. Lower-level claims need assessability.
review_prompts: Is a high-level claim overloaded with low-level detail?
Is a leaf claim too vague to assess against evidence?
Could the claim stay short because linked criteria already make it objective?
guidelines.statement: Keep upper-level claims short and stable; make evidence-facing claims precise enough to assess.
guidelines.title: Match claim precision to the level of the argument

detection_hints: Look for top-level claims overloaded with measurement detail.
Look for leaf claims too vague to compare with evidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claim precision matches argument level.

guidelines.rationale: Silent redefinition can leave higher-level claims only partially supported while appearing complete.
review_prompts: Does a key term mean the same thing at parent and sub-claim levels?
Has scope narrowed without being stated?
Is inherited context still valid at this level?
guidelines.statement: Do not silently redefine the object, scope, or meaning of key terms as the argument decomposes.
guidelines.title: Keep scope and terminology consistent across decomposition

detection_hints: Look for parent/child pairs where a key noun's scope changes silently.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether key terms preserve scope across decomposition.

guidelines.rationale: This guideline is about whether the branch contains enough context at all. In GSN, claims are asserted in a specified context. A claim that lacks essential context can look stronger than intended or become hard to review consistently because different readers may supply different meanings or boundaries.
review_prompts: What must the reviewer know for this claim to be true or false?
Are key terms defined where needed?
Is any necessary scope or operating condition explicit?
Would two independent reviewers understand the claim in the same way?
guidelines.statement: Provide the context needed for the reviewer to understand the claim’s subject, intended meaning, scope, operating conditions, and key definitions.
guidelines.title: Provide the context needed to interpret the claim

detection_hints: Look for claims using domain terms that are not defined in any linked context.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim has enough linked context for consistent interpretation.

guidelines.rationale: This guideline is about placement, clarity, and maintainability. Hidden qualifiers blur element roles, make scope and dependency changes harder to see, and often create claims that are difficult to review and maintain.
review_prompts: Which words in this claim are qualifiers rather than the core assertion?
Are the qualifiers clear enough for review, or would they be better represented as context or assumptions?
Could the core claim remain stable if a configuration, interface condition, or dependency changed?
Are dependencies explicit and traceable rather than hidden inside readable but overloaded claim text?
guidelines.statement: Do not hide qualifiers, definitions, interface conditions, or dependency clauses in claim text in a way that obscures scope or support. Use separate context or assumption structures where available; otherwise make the qualifiers deliberate, clear, and consistently phrased.
guidelines.title: Make claim qualifiers explicit and maintainable

detection_hints: Look for connectives in claim text such as with, given, assuming, provided that, when.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether qualifying clauses in claim text should move to context or assumption elements.

guidelines.rationale: Rationale can explain local reasoning choices, but it cannot replace sub-claims, evidence, or a clear argument linking evidence to the claim. Treating rationale as support hides missing reasoning, missing evidence, or unsupported assumptions.
review_prompts: Is the rationale explaining a local choice, or trying to carry evidential weight?
If the rationale were removed, would the real support for the claim still remain?
guidelines.statement: Use rationale, warrant, or justification text to explain why a wording, boundary, decomposition, or inference choice is acceptable; do not use it as the proof that a claim is true.
guidelines.title: Do not use rationale as hidden support

detection_hints: Look for justifications that cite test results or evidence rather than rationale.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the justification carries evidential weight that should sit in evidence or sub-claims.

guidelines.rationale: Misaligned rationale creates false confidence and often reveals that the real concern is missing context, missing decomposition, missing evidence, or an unstated inference rule.
review_prompts: Does the rationale explain why this exact claim formulation, decomposition, or inference is acceptable?
Is it local, or is it trying to justify the whole branch?
Could the same text be pasted onto many different elements without change?
guidelines.statement: Any rationale, warrant, or justification shall address the exact claim, argument, or inference step to which it is attached and shall not explain a different issue elsewhere in the branch.
guidelines.title: Match each rationale to the element or inference it explains

detection_hints: Look for justifications that could be moved to other elements without losing meaning.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the justification is local to its attached element.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case without traceability cannot be effectively reviewed or maintained.
review_prompts: Can the reviewer identify the intended evidence path without having to infer it?
Is it clear which evidence path ultimately supports this claim?
Would two reviewers follow the same trace to the same evidence?
guidelines.statement: Show, for each claim, the evidence path that supports it, either directly or through stated sub-claims and intermediate arguments.
guidelines.title: Make the evidence-support path explicit for every claim

detection_hints: Look for claims with no traceable path to evidence.
Look for solutions linked to claims without intermediate sub-claims when needed.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each claim has an explicit evidence path through sub-claims or direct solutions.

guidelines.rationale: A reviewer should be able to recognize what kind of evidence is being used, what makes it acceptable for this purpose, and how it should be interpreted. If an artifact is not an approved evidence type, or does not meet the criteria required for that type, it becomes difficult to review consistently and easy to misuse in a safety argument.
review_prompts: Is the evidence type clearly defined?
Is the expected structure or content of the artifact defined?
Is it clear how the artifact is to be interpreted?
Is there a defined basis for reviewing, validating, or accepting this evidence type?
Could an independent reviewer examine the artifact consistently without relying on undocumented local knowledge?
guidelines.statement: Do not use evidence unless its artifact type is defined for safety case use and the artifact meets the criteria required for that type, so that it can be reviewed and assessed consistently.
guidelines.title: Use evidence types that can be independently reviewed

detection_hints: Look for evidence references to ad-hoc or working artifacts (working file, draft notes).

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the evidence type is defined and the artifact meets the type's criteria.

guidelines.rationale: Evidence usually supports a specific fact or bounded property, not the whole safety conclusion by itself.
review_prompts: Is the goal naming a document instead of a supported property?
Is the evidential link too large for the cited artifact?
Would the claim remain meaningful if the artifact name changed?
guidelines.statement: Write the claim as the fact or property being supported; do not make the goal say that a report, analysis, or test proves the safety conclusion.
guidelines.title: Claim the fact supported by the evidence, not the document

detection_hints: Look for claim text that names a report, document, or analysis as the subject.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the claim subject is a property rather than a document.

guidelines.rationale: Broad references to whole reports create the illusion of support without making the evidential link easy to review.
review_prompts: Could a reviewer find the relevant support quickly?
Is the cited location precise enough?
Is the reference proportionate to the actual support being used?
guidelines.statement: Reference the exact section, figure, table, dataset, or artifact portion that supports the claim when practical.
guidelines.title: Cite precise evidence locations; avoid annex dumping

detection_hints: Look for evidence references that name an entire report without section/table/figure.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether evidence references are specific enough to be quickly verified.

guidelines.rationale: A reviewer should not have to guess why a cited test, analysis, dataset, or review record is enough. The argument should make the sufficiency basis visible, such as relevant scope, configuration, scenario coverage, thresholds, acceptance conditions, and known limitations.
review_prompts: What makes this evidence enough for this claim?
Is the required scope, configuration, scenario set, or operating condition clear?
Is any threshold, pass criterion, or completeness expectation stated?
Are known limitations or uncovered conditions explicit?
Is the branch showing only that the evidence is relevant, or also that it is enough?
guidelines.statement: When a claim is supported by evidence, make clear what makes that evidence sufficient for that claim.
guidelines.title: Make the basis for evidence sufficiency explicit

detection_hints: Look for evidence cited without scope, threshold, or coverage justification.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the basis for evidence sufficiency is explicit.

guidelines.rationale: Evidence does not speak for itself. The safety case or linked assessment record must explain why the evidence bears on the claim.
review_prompts: Is it explicit why this evidence matters for this claim?
Is the inferential link documented in a reviewable form?
Does the documentation explain only support, or also limitations and possible refutation?
Has confirmation bias been considered?
guidelines.statement: Ensure the inferential link between claim and evidence is explicitly documented and reviewable. The documentation shall explain how the cited evidence supports the claim, and where relevant how it reveals limitations or possible refutation.
guidelines.title: Explain how the evidence supports or refutes the claim

detection_hints: Look for evidence linked to claims without an accompanying inferential explanation.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the inferential link between claim and evidence is reviewable.

guidelines.rationale: Uncontrolled or mutable evidence is hard to verify, maintain, and re-assess. If a cited artifact can change after review, the argument may silently lose validity while still appearing supported.
review_prompts: Who owns the evidence?
Which version or revision is being cited?
Is the evidence retrieved from a controlled location?
Is the cited artifact fixed, or can it still change?
If it is a live document, is there an explicit mechanism that re-assesses affected claims when the document changes?
Is its status clear, for example draft, in review, approved, or released?
guidelines.statement: Evidence cited in the safety case should be under configuration or document control, with clear ownership, version or revision, date, status, and a stable retrieval location. Do not rely on mutable live documents as evidence unless the cited version is fixed or the change process explicitly triggers re-assessment of the affected claim.
guidelines.title: Keep evidence controlled: owner, version, date, status, repository

detection_hints: Look for evidence references with no version, date, owner, or controlled location.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each evidence reference includes owner, version, date, status, and stable location (directly or via linked control mechanism).

guidelines.rationale: This rule is the specific citation case of EV.7. If cited evidence can change after review, the safety case may appear supported while its actual evidential basis has changed or disappeared. This breaks reproducibility, reviewability, and configuration control.
review_prompts: Could this cited content change without the safety case being updated?
Is the cited state fixed, versioned, or archived?
Can a future reviewer retrieve the exact same content that was reviewed?
If the source is live, is there an explicit process that triggers re-assessment of affected claims when it changes?
guidelines.statement: Do not cite live mutable content as evidence unless the cited state is fixed, versioned, archived, or otherwise controlled so that the reviewed argument always refers to the same content.
guidelines.title: Cite fixed evidence, not live mutable content

detection_hints: Look for citations to wikis, live shared docs, or other mutable URLs without a fixed version or snapshot.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the cited content state is fixed, versioned, or archived.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case should argue from reviewable evidence, not from what engineers happen to know. When system knowledge is written directly into the safety case without a supporting source, the argument becomes hard to verify, hard to maintain, and difficult to assess for completeness. It also becomes unclear whether the claim is supported by an approved design basis or only by current team understanding.
review_prompts: Is this claim supported by controlled documentation or other identified evidence?
Is the safety case describing how the system works instead of arguing from documented sources?
Would the claim still be supportable if the original engineer were unavailable?
Should this material be moved to a specification, design description, interface definition, hazard analysis, or other work product and then cited as evidence?
guidelines.statement: Do not support claims by relying on undocumented engineering knowledge, design understanding, or verbal explanation. Claims about system behavior, design, interfaces, mitigations, or operating limits should be grounded in controlled documentation or other identified evidence.
guidelines.title: Do not argue directly from undocumented system knowledge

detection_hints: Look for free-text design explanations in the safety case without linked specification or evidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the argument relies on undocumented system knowledge rather than cited artifacts.

guidelines.rationale: A credible safety case should not only present supporting material. It should also make important doubts visible and show how they are handled. This fits well with GSN-style review, where challenge is used to test whether a claim, inference, or supporting material still stands when subjected to scrutiny.
review_prompts: What could invalidate this claim or reasoning step?
What assumptions, confounders, uncertainties, or biases are relevant here?
Could this evidence be incomplete, misleading, or outside the supported scope?
Is the challenge really against the claim, the reasoning, the evidence, an assumption, or the stated scope?
Are important doubts visible in the argument, or left unstated?
guidelines.statement: Where a reviewer could reasonably question whether a claim, reasoning step, evidence item, assumption, or stated scope is valid, complete, applicable, or sufficiently reliable, make that challenge explicit and address it where needed.
guidelines.title: Identify and address plausible challenges to claims, reasoning, and evidence

detection_hints: Look for branches presenting only supporting material with no challenges or responses.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether plausible reviewer challenges to the claim, reasoning, or evidence are visible and addressed.

guidelines.rationale: Unstated or weakly founded assumptions are a common cause of later argument invalidation. That aligns well with UL 4600’s treatment of assumptions and lifecycle monitoring. GSN also treats assumptions as a distinct element type, so checking whether something is really an assumption is appropriate.
review_prompts: What must be true for this branch to hold?
Why is this assumption reasonable, and how would we know if it became false?
Is this really an assumption, or should it instead be represented as context, a claim, or evidence?
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on hidden assumptions. State assumptions explicitly, explain why they are reasonable, and ensure they are monitored or otherwise controlled where needed.
guidelines.title: Make assumptions explicit and justify why they are reasonable

detection_hints: Look for branches whose validity depends on a condition that is not stated as an assumption or context.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether implicit assumptions are made explicit, justified, and monitorable.

guidelines.rationale: Expert opinion may be useful, but unsupported opinion is weak support and can easily outstate what is actually known.
review_prompts: Is the opinion supported by data, literature, documented analysis, or another explicit technical basis?
Is the context of applicability clear and argued?
If the opinion remains weakly supported, is lifecycle monitoring in place where needed?
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on expert judgment alone unless its basis, limits, and corroborating support are stated, or the residual uncertainty is monitored over the lifecycle where appropriate.
guidelines.title: Do not rely on uncorroborated expert judgment alone

detection_hints: Look for evidence consisting only of expert statements without supporting analysis or data.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether expert judgment is corroborated by data, analysis, or lifecycle monitoring.

guidelines.rationale: Some claims depend partly on assumptions, limited evidence, or expected field behavior. In such cases, the safety case should not hide the remaining uncertainty. It should explain it and define how operation will provide feedback.
review_prompts: What part of this claim is not fully supported at design time?
Can that remaining uncertainty only be reduced through operational or field data?
Is lifecycle monitoring defined for that uncertainty?
Are reassessment triggers identified?
guidelines.statement: When a claim cannot be fully supported at design time, make the remaining uncertainty explicit and define lifecycle monitoring that can confirm or challenge the claim during operation.
guidelines.title: Monitor claims that cannot be fully supported at design time

detection_hints: Look for claims with partial design-time support and no defined lifecycle monitoring.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims with residual design-time uncertainty have defined monitoring and reassessment triggers.

guidelines.rationale: Safety confidence gained in one context does not automatically remain valid in another. Differences in operating environment, purpose, interfaces, duty cycle, autonomy role, or assumptions can invalidate the reuse.
review_prompts: What safety confidence, evidence, or assessment result is being reused from another context?
Is the original operating context sufficiently comparable to the current one?
Have differences in purpose, environment, interfaces, or assumptions been identified?
Have the limitations of the original assessment been stated?
guidelines.statement: Do not rely on safety credit from proven-in-use technology, legacy technology, COTS, prior assessments, standard conformance, or prior practice unless you show that the original context is sufficiently comparable to the current one.
guidelines.title: Do not reuse safety credit from another context without showing it still applies

detection_hints: Look for proven-in-use or legacy claims with no comparability argument.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether reused safety credit is supported by an explicit comparability argument.

guidelines.rationale: Operational feedback is often used to support claims about residual risk, rarity, adequacy of existing controls, or continued acceptability in service. In those branches, non-injury or non-reproducibility does not make a signal irrelevant. Several weak signals together may show that the argument is less reliable than it appears.
review_prompts: Is this branch relying on operational experience or field feedback as part of its support?
Are incidents defined broadly enough to include near misses, close calls, and anomalies that could have led to harm?
Is adverse operational feedback being screened out too aggressively?
Is the argument considering the combined signal from multiple incidents or anomalies?
Is adverse operational evidence explicitly recorded, evaluated, and addressed?
guidelines.statement: When a claim relies on operational experience, field monitoring, incident history, or proven-in-use style reasoning, do not dismiss incidents, near misses, anomalies, or failure reports merely because they have not recurred, cannot yet be reproduced, or did not lead to harm.
guidelines.title: Do not dismiss operational feedback because it is non-reproducible or non-injury

detection_hints: Look for arguments that use operational data and discount non-injury or non-reproducible incidents.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether adverse operational feedback is recorded, grouped, and evaluated rather than silently dismissed.

guidelines.rationale: Operational exposure can miss catastrophic but rare outcomes. Simulation can miss modeling defects and abstraction errors.
review_prompts: Is simulation alone being treated as enough to show low risk?
Is operational history alone being treated as enough to show low risk?
Has simulation validity for this claim not been shown?
Are corroborating evidence, scenario limits, or model limitations missing?
guidelines.statement: Do not infer low risk for a known hazard solely from uneventful operational history or from simulation whose credibility for the claim has not been demonstrated.
guidelines.title: Do not argue low risk from operational experience or unvalidated simulation alone

detection_hints: Look for low-risk claims supported only by simulation or only by uneventful operational time.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether low-risk claims combine multiple corroborating evidence types and address simulation validity.

guidelines.rationale: Autonomous systems can encounter operating situations and failure combinations that are uncommon in human driving. Human-derived data and human-designed tests may therefore miss important autonomy-specific risks.
review_prompts: Is the claim supported mainly by human-operated data or human-designed tests?
Could the autonomous system encounter situations or create hazards that are uncommon in human driving?
Are autonomy-specific failure modes and edge cases explicitly considered?
Is there evidence that the test basis covers autonomy-specific failures, not only human-driving situations?
guidelines.statement: Do not assume that human-operated data sets or human-designed test plans are sufficient to cover autonomy-specific failures or edge cases.
guidelines.title: Do not assume human data or human-designed tests cover autonomy-specific failures

detection_hints: Look for claims about autonomy coverage backed only by human-driven datasets or human-designed scenarios.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether the test basis covers autonomy-specific failure modes and edge cases.

guidelines.rationale: Hidden dependencies are a common reason for late argument invalidation. Making them visible helps the reviewer see what the branch depends on and decide whether that dependency should remain an assumption, be stated as context, or be argued as a claim.
review_prompts: What must be true for this claim or strategy to hold, but is not currently stated?
Is the hidden dependency local to the claim, or to the reasoning step?
Should this dependency be represented as an assumption, as context, or as a claim that must be proved?
guidelines.statement: When a claim or reasoning step depends on something that is not currently stated, make that dependency explicit at the point where it constrains the argument, using an assumption, context element, or subclaim as appropriate.
guidelines.title: Document unstated assumptions at the point of use

detection_hints: Look for claims whose validity depends on conditions not stated as assumption, context, or subclaim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether unstated dependencies are made visible at the point of use.

guidelines.rationale: Over-broad assumptions can make a claim appear closed while removing most of its review value. If an argument depends on an assumption, the assumption should be narrow enough to understand, evaluate, and monitor where needed.
review_prompts: Is the assumption matched to the scope of the claim it constrains?
Can the assumption be checked, challenged, or monitored?
Does the assumption hide several different dependencies that should be separated?
Would the branch become clearer if the assumption were narrowed or split?
guidelines.statement: Do not use assumptions that are broader than the claim scope or so vague that they cannot be checked, challenged, or monitored.
guidelines.title: Keep assumptions bounded, specific, and monitorable

detection_hints: Look for assumptions that are vague, universal, or unmonitorable.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each assumption is narrow, specific, and monitorable where needed.

guidelines.rationale: A credible safety case should not leave plausible challenges only in review comments or reviewer intuition. Good reviews expose weaknesses early. Making the challenge explicit helps ensure that it is either resolved properly or left visible until it is resolved.
review_prompts: What exactly is the reviewer challenge?
Should this challenge be made explicit as a Counter Claim, defeater, or other challenge element?
Has the challenge been rejected, sustained, or left unresolved?
If sustained, has the original branch been updated appropriately?
If unresolved, is the open issue visible and traceable?
guidelines.statement: When review raises a plausible What if X? challenge, make that challenge explicit and resolve it visibly in the safety case. Depending on the method, this may be represented as a GSN Counter Claim, a CAE defeater, or another explicit challenge element. The resolution may reject the challenge, narrow or revise the original claim, add supporting evidence, introduce assumptions and monitoring, or leave a visible open issue if the matter is not yet resolved.
guidelines.title: Make plausible reviewer challenges explicit and resolve them

detection_hints: Look for plausible reviewer challenges that have not been promoted into the safety case.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether plausible reviewer challenges are made explicit and visibly resolved.

guidelines.rationale: Circular support creates the appearance of argument without adding any new support.
review_prompts: Would the support still work if the parent claim were not assumed true?
Is the same conclusion being repeated with different words?
guidelines.statement: Do not support a claim by restating it, renaming it, or assuming it in the support.
guidelines.title: Avoid circular reasoning

detection_hints: Look for support that restates or renames the parent claim.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether support adds independent reasoning or merely restates the claim.

guidelines.rationale: A common defect is to attach true or relevant material to the wrong claim, so the branch appears supported even though the actual inference is missing.
review_prompts: Does this evidence support this exact claim?
Is the evidence only relevant to a different or neighboring claim?
Is the missing support actually a different intermediate claim that has not been stated?
guidelines.statement: Do not use evidence or supporting statements that may be true but do not support the immediate claim being made.
guidelines.title: Avoid irrelevant premises

detection_hints: Look for evidence whose actual scope supports a different claim than the one it is attached to.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each evidence item supports the immediate claim it is attached to.

guidelines.rationale: Not finding a problem is not the same as showing that the problem does not exist. Claims about completeness or absence need support from the search basis, scope, and adequacy of the methods used.
review_prompts: Is not found being treated as does not exist?
Is the claim really about completeness of the search, rather than absolute absence?
Was the search for contrary evidence demonstrably adequate for the stated scope?
guidelines.statement: Do not treat lack of discovered evidence against a claim as positive evidence for the claim.
guidelines.title: Avoid arguing from ignorance

detection_hints: Look for completeness or absence claims justified only by absence-of-finding.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether absence-based claims are reframed as bounded completeness claims with adequate search coverage.

guidelines.rationale: Comparison-based arguments can look persuasive while hiding differences in scope, operating conditions, metrics, evidence quality, or confidence. Distinctions can also be misused to dismiss relevant comparators without showing why the difference matters.
review_prompts: What exactly is being compared or distinguished?
Is the basis of comparison or distinction explicit?
Are the compared cases matched in scope, operating conditions, metrics, and confidence level?
If a difference is claimed, is it shown why that difference matters to the argument?
guidelines.statement: Do not claim that one case is equivalent to, safer than, better than, or different from another unless the basis of comparison or distinction is explicit and relevant to the claim being made.
guidelines.title: Avoid unjustified comparison or unjustified distinction

detection_hints: Look for safer-than or different-from claims without an explicit basis of comparison.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether comparisons or distinctions are matched in scope, conditions, metrics, and confidence.

guidelines.rationale: A small or skewed data set can support only a correspondingly narrow claim.
review_prompts: Is the sample size adequate for the confidence implied?
Does the data distribution match the ODD and edge cases?
Is the claim broader than the sample supports?
guidelines.statement: Do not generalize too far from too little data, or from data that does not match the operating context being claimed.
guidelines.title: Avoid sample-size and representativeness fallacies

detection_hints: Look for broad claims supported by narrow or small data sets.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether sample size and representativeness match the breadth of the claim.

guidelines.rationale: A highly precise number can give a false impression of certainty. When uncertainty, confidence, model limits, or input assumptions are weak, the stated precision should reflect that.
review_prompts: Does the number imply a level of certainty the method cannot support?
Are uncertainty, assumptions, and confidence bounds stated where needed?
Is the stated precision greater than the quality of the underlying evidence or model?
Would a rounded value or bounded statement better reflect the real knowledge state?
guidelines.statement: Do not present numerical precision beyond what the evidence, model, assumptions, or method can justify.
guidelines.title: Avoid pseudo-precision

detection_hints: Look for many-significant-digit numerical claims without uncertainty or confidence statement.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether numerical precision is consistent with model and data uncertainty.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case becomes misleading when it presents only supporting material and leaves out evidence that could weaken, limit, or challenge the claim.
review_prompts: What evidence would a critical reviewer reasonably expect to see for this claim?
Is any known anomaly, failure, exclusion, or limitation being left unaddressed?
Does the omitted material affect the meaning, scope, or credibility of the claim?
Is contrary evidence explicitly addressed rather than silently ignored?
guidelines.statement: Do not omit evidence that a skeptical reviewer would naturally expect, and do not leave known contrary evidence unanswered.
guidelines.title: Avoid omission of key evidence and ignoring counter-evidence

detection_hints: Look for branches that present only supporting evidence with no acknowledgement of known limits or contrary evidence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether known limiting or contrary evidence is addressed or scoped out.

guidelines.rationale: Review becomes harder when the reader must infer the role of a statement. Clear signposting reduces confusion between argument elements and makes the structure easier to inspect.
review_prompts: Is the reader forced to infer the role of the statement?
Are claims, context, assumptions, and justifications mixed together?
Is evidence clearly identifiable as evidence rather than explanation or claim text?
guidelines.statement: Make it clear whether a statement is functioning as a claim, evidence reference, context, assumption, or justification.
guidelines.title: Use explicit signposting of argument element roles

detection_hints: Look for prose statements that mix claim, context, assumption, and evidence in one sentence.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether each statement is clearly signposted with its argument element role.

guidelines.rationale: Safety cases should communicate justified confidence, not absolute assurance when support is partial, bounded, or still open in some respects.
review_prompts: Is the scope of the claim explicit?
Is unresolved uncertainty visible?
Does the wording overstate closure?
Does the confidence language match the actual support?
guidelines.statement: State the operating scope and use confidence language that reflects the actual support and any open issues.
guidelines.title: Use scoped claims and qualified confidence language

detection_hints: Look for unscoped claims using absolute confidence language (is safe, is correct).

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims state operating scope and use confidence language matched to actual support.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case is easier to review and trust when it shows not only supporting material, but also the important limits and challenges that affect confidence in the claim.
review_prompts: Are important limitations visible at the point where they affect the claim?
Are plausible objections or challenges addressed explicitly?
Is unresolved doubt hidden, or made visible through scope restriction, assumptions, monitoring, or open issues?
guidelines.statement: Make relevant limitations, plausible objections, and uncertainty sources explicit, together with how they are addressed in the argument.
guidelines.title: Make limitations, objections, and responses explicit

detection_hints: Look for claims with no visible limitation, exclusion, or open issue despite known partial coverage.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether known limitations and objections are visible at the point of the affected claim.

guidelines.rationale: Safety arguments should build confidence through explicit claims, reasoning, and evidence, not through language intended to impress the reader.
review_prompts: Does the wording sound promotional rather than argumentative?
Would the sentence lose nothing important if the praise-like wording were removed?
Is the wording trying to create confidence through tone rather than support?
guidelines.statement: Do not use promotional, boastful, or image-enhancing language in the safety case.
guidelines.title: Avoid promotional and inflated language

detection_hints: Look for promotional adjectives such as world-class, cutting-edge, outstanding, best-in-class.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether claims use promotional or image-enhancing language.

guidelines.rationale: When a review, judgment, approval, or decision is stated without naming who performed it, accountability becomes harder to inspect and challenge.
review_prompts: Who performed the review, judgment, or approval?
Does the wording hide who is responsible?
Would naming the actor improve traceability or auditability?
guidelines.statement: Do not use passive wording when the identity of the actor matters to understanding, reviewing, or challenging the argument.
guidelines.title: Avoid passive voice when it hides agency

detection_hints: Look for it was determined / has been reviewed / is considered without a named actor.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether reviews, judgments, and approvals name the responsible actor.

guidelines.rationale: A safety case should make important boundaries visible where the claim is read. If key limitations or assumptions are easy to miss, the claim can appear stronger or broader than the argument really supports.
review_prompts: Is an important limitation easy to miss?
Is an important assumption stated explicitly as an assumption, or only implied elsewhere?
Would a reviewer be misled by reading only the main branch?
Should the limitation or dependency be made visible through context, an assumption, or a narrower claim?
guidelines.statement: Do not hide important limitations or assumptions in appendices, footnotes, or free text that is not directly connected to the claim they qualify.
guidelines.title: Do not bury important limitations or hidden assumptions

detection_hints: Look for important limiting conditions stated only in appendices or distant free text.

suggested_checks.description: Check whether important limitations and assumptions are visible where the claim is read.
